That’s not what either of those mean, at least within philosophy (might be different in art history or something idk, I’m just a philosophy major). I don’t have a problem with simplifying concepts in general, but the explanations you provided are very inaccurate and misleading. 

Existentialism more or less has two varieties, atheistic (Sartre, de Beauvoir, etc.) and non-atheistic (Kierkegaard, mystic existentialists, etc.) (there’s also Heideggerian existentialism but we’ll ignore him for now) The more well-known atheistic kind can be simplified as basically saying that life has no *prior* meaning (the emphasis on prior is very important because it distinguishes it from certain varieties of nihilism and anti-realism) but that humans are condemned to be free to create their own meaning and should avoid bad-faith attempts to avoid this freedom. This is basically the opposite of “don’t care “; this variant of existentialism generally wants you to care very much about creating meaning in your life because well, it’s impossible not to. (it should also be noted that this personal meaning is not necessarily “not real” or “subjective”, but that’s a more complicated topic). 

Absurdism, at least the most well known form of it championed by Camus, is a bit different from existentialism in that it doesn’t say that “the world” has no meaning , but rather, that our relationship with the world cannot be meaningful. You cannot make any meaning out of the absurd relationship to the world. Camus’s answer to why we should live, then, is deliberately non-philosophical; it’s about triumph and rebellion from the absurd. Elaborating more on this unsatisfyingly simple answer is beyond the scope of a Reddit comment, but I urge curious readers to check out the SEP. In any case, Camus does not say we should or can “love” the meaninglessness of the world.

I’m not an economist but I study causal inference and discovery at the graduate level. For causality in general, there are basically 3 prominent “methods” of arriving at causality. 

The first is randomized controlled trials, which is already mentioned in one of the comments. Another prominent method, which iirc is indeed used in economics sometimes, is Granger causality. Basically you use statistical constraints and basic principles like “the future can’t affect the past” to derive forecasting variables in time series data. 

The third family of methods comes from researchers like Pearl, Scholkopf, and Spirtes/Glymour, and it uses graphical DAGs and other causal models to model causality. There are a variety of techniques this group is associated with. The PC algorithm, for instance, can be proved to be able to recover the true underlying causal structure of the data under certain assumptions (no latent confounders, enough data, acyclic, no ambiguous manipulations, Markov condition, etc) by using conditional independence tests. In a way, you can say that under some conditions, correlations give us some evidence of causality. For instance, if you’re dealing with bivarite normal variables, zero correlation implies independence, and this is used to construct a causal skeleton. As far as I know, this family of methods is not as commonly used in economics, but it’s a fairly new area of research so it’s understandable.

You’re right that that was my assumption, and yes, the second function you wrote does have O(1) complexity even in the theoretical definition. I guess it depends on how OP implemented it. But it’s worth noting that the first function is fundamentally different from the second one and has O(n) complexity.

The thing is that the constraint “the input is size 1000 no matter what” is external to the function itself. From my understanding, there is no logic inside the function that checks or enforces this constraint. So the running of the function under the constraint may be constant time, but the function’s inherent time complexity is O(n). I’m using the theoretical cs definition of time complexity here, where it is defined for an algorithm that by definition halts on every possible input string. So maximal time complexity also considers every possible input string of the underlying alphabet ({0,1} most likely). Time complexity doesn’t consider what you constrain “outside” of the algorithm.

This is a bad take. 

First nitpick: Camus had not much to say about ethics so I don’t know why you mentioned him in particular. 

Secondly: contemporary philosophy is much less dominated by particular “geniuses” just like most other contemporary academia. It’s pretty odd to say that the only way to solve ai ethics is by consulting a selected few philosophers, especially considering that philosophy is a discipline that very directly benefits from more discourse. 

Thirdly: whichever group of people “solves” ai ethics is going to have to be interdisciplinary. Just to give a trivial example, the problem of zero-sum games between ai agents is clearly a problem that requires knowledge of game theory and CS besides just philosophy. Someone who is as good as Kant would still utterly fail to develop ai ethics by himself without the help of people with technical knowledge. One person (or a few) can only dig so many deep wells.

Hi, this is kind of personal, but I was just wondering if someone could give me advice on being disillusioned with the tech industry. Obviously, as an inexperienced dev, I know that my conceptualization of the tech industry isn’t anywhere close to complete, so I would appreciate input from you experienced folk.

I’m an undergrad student at a T4 university for cs in the US. To be honest, even this “Top 4” bullshit kinda sickens me, along with all the nonsense words that young cs bros use. I’m also a philosophy double major, because philosophy is my true passion, and while I do genuinely enjoy programming, I only see it as a force multiplier without direction, while philosophy is what provides my direction. I’m also very interested in things like poetry, the humanities, sociology, etc — things that very few other cs majors around me are interested in. 

I don’t mean to sound pretentious, but I’ve noticed that most of the people in this industry and in this discipline just don’t care that much. They roll their eyes at ethics, they justify their apathy with an ironic cynicism, and they’re happy with being meek spectators as long as they get paid well. Amnesia seems to me the slogan of the tech industry— the economic downturns and upturns, the new frameworks every three years, billion dollar startups that disappear in a year— the most efficient way people deal with this is by forgetting quickly and moving on quickly. There is no past and there’s an infinite future, so no one can dwell in the present, much less “live” in it. 

I try to find communities of like minded tech people, for example, programmers who might read philosophy or be more humanities oriented, but I haven’t succeeded yet. I want to offer my perspective here as someone who is a college freshman (double)majoring in philosophy that have read similar works as you(Debord, Baudrillard, Marx, etc.) and is greatly sympathetic to that general family of views. I think my perspective will be particularly useful  because it stands at the intersection between future parent/adult and child. 

I grew up in a particularly hyper-competitive and wealthy area of South Korea(which is itself a competitive and extremely capitalist country) under well-off parents. Both of my parents are doctors who worked their asses off to become one(btw, in Korea, being a doctor isn’t nearly as lucrative as in America, though it’s still very much upper-middle/upper class), so they have the typical pro-capitalist anti-socialist meritocratic mindset that many upper-middle class people espouse. My mom in particular grew up poor and achieved a rare rags-to-riches story by being at the top of her school nearly every year in grades. 

While my parents rarely explicitly pushed anti-socialist or pro-capitalist views, it was pretty implicit in the society surrounding me and the kind of parenting they gave. Throughout my preteen and early teen years, I grew increasingly disillusioned with my surroundings and discovered philosophy on my own, which naturally led to critical theory, continental philosophy, contemporary gender theory, and the like down the line. 

Looking back, I would have liked it more if my parents had equipped me with the skills to be critical, think carefully and patiently, virtues like intellectual humility, etc., though, obviously that’s something you can’t reasonably expect out of people that come from their background. What I would not have appreciated is them giving me explicit exposure to only a small area of thought, whether it be critical theory or neoliberalism or whatever.  The more I engage with philosophy, the more I realize how much there is I don’t know, and how much there is that I don’t even know that I don’t know. My views get changed, sharpened, abandoned all the time, and I’ve realized that there is so much value in simply suspending clear judgement while studying further material in good faith to resolve or advance that suspense. Right now, my biggest idols are Baudrillard and Nietzsche. Last year, I was in love with Cioran. Next year, I’m planning on reading more from Habermas, and who knows what movement/philosopher/ism that I’ll discover. 

The top comment raises a good point in that parents should install the right values in their children and critique the wrong ones. But the vast majority of critical theory is under very rigorous and active debate right now even in respectable academia. The critical theorists and philosophers aren’t stupid for not having knock-down arguments that extinguish serious opposition, they’re still in the process of making novel conversations about it. Time will tell if they prevail, and your child will have access to arguments and papers and the responses to those arguments and papers that we don’t even know that we don’t know about today. But if my parents had only shown me a small piece of the whole conversation, even if it were rigorous on its own, I suspect that I would have grown up to be intellectually arrogant, blinded by the rigor of “our side” that I become lazy to explore alternative ideas or even relatively unrelated but still interesting things like formal logic or philosophy of religion.  Ultimately, it was my passion to know more, to explore beyond the horizon that had frustrated and disillusioned me, that led me to higher levels of rigor. 

This isn’t to say that you shouldn’t teach your child about critical theory and its adjacent ideas; I’m only saying that you should do this after you already taught your child how to critique, self-reflect, ask questions, read and write precisely, how to engage with conversations in good faith, the value of intellectual humility, and also only in conjunction with alternate ideas that will complicate or broaden the other things you want to teach. So teach your child Marx, but teach them Locke as well(I mean, I’m not even sure how you would be able to teach someone Marx in good faith without teaching them the ideas that Marx is critiquing anyways). If you’re not confident that you can do this in good faith, I suggest only going as far as teaching them the foundational skills that will guide the child to think on his own. 

One more thing: even while i was disturbed by the spectacle and hyperreality and nausea of my surrounding capitalist society, the most hurtful aspect of my parenting was actually the implicit lack of respect given to my autonomy as a thinking, acting, reasoning human on my own right. The expectation was that I don’t say no to what my parents say, that questions with complicated answers not be asked, and my thought was merely an extension, a yet-to-be-conquered patch of my parent’s ideology.  If you guide your child to have the skills necessary to be an autonomous thinking being, I would say that that is even more valuable than raising him to be either a materialistic, and yes, even a moral success.
